scenario: A blog post's impressions rose 40% this month. The team reports this as proof that the on-page content is now more engaging and readers are spending more time on it.
A page ranking #2 has a 22% CTR. The analyst compares it only against other pages ranking in positions 1-3, not against a site-wide average CTR, before deciding it is underperforming.

The monthly report shows organic clicks and CTR in one section, and time-on-page, scroll depth, and email signups in a clearly separate section, so a reader can see traffic grew while engagement dipped.

A page ranking #14 gets a new headline that lifts its CTR by 3 points. The team prioritizes rolling this same headline test out to the site's top pages ranking #1-3 first, expecting the biggest absolute click gain there.
A post's organic clicks dropped for one week, then bounced back the following week. The editor immediately flags it for a full content refresh based on that single week's dip.

A decayed post's pricing and screenshots are outdated. The writer updates the facts and screenshots, re-verifies the stats against current sources, and updates the visible and structured-data modification date to match.

A post has sustained decay, but its facts are still accurate — it has simply been outranked by newer, more thorough competitor content. The team responds by only changing the 'last updated' date on the page without adding any new depth or evidence.
Before refreshing a decayed post, the writer re-checks every carried-over statistic against its current primary source, exactly as they would for a brand-new post.
A headline A/B test starts trending significant on day 2 of a planned 14-day run. The team stops the test immediately and ships the winning headline as the new default.

A test needs an early check due to a hard business deadline, so the team uses an always-valid confidence-sequence method built for continuous monitoring rather than a fixed-sample p-value check at an arbitrary interim point.
One experiment simultaneously varies the headline and the CTA copy in the same arm, while also letting the page's ranking position shift between the two variants.
A test reaches its pre-committed sample size and stopping rule with a clear winner. The team reports that variant as the new default headline.
Marketing publishes 'proven to double clicks' in a stakeholder deck based on a mid-test lift observed on day 3 of a test that has not yet reached its pre-committed stopping rule.
After refreshing a post, the team updates the byline, publish date, and last-reviewed date in both the visible page and the structured data before marking the refresh complete.
